# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act - DLA Piper GENIE

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
1200 19th Street NW, Suite 400, Washington, DC 20036

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and compute infrastructure on which American leadership in AI depends.

Thank you for releasing a genuinely bipartisan draft, and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. We know how difficult that is on this issue. We also want to be clear about where we stand, because our support and our opposition run through the same bill.

**Summary of our position.** We strongly support Section 121, the federalization of state laws regulating AI model development, and we ask you to make it permanent. We ask you to strike Subtitle B's reporting and audit regime (Sections 111 and 112), strike the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and its $100 million annual authorization (Section 102), and ask appropriators to defund CAISI. We support the workforce, cybersecurity, research and fraud-deterrence provisions in Titles II through IV. Our objection is not to federal action. It is to a federal regime built on an unfounded premise.

**1. The draft writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code.**

Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk," "critical safety incident," "loss of control" and "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Those four definitions are the load-bearing walls of the bill. Every obligation, audit and penalty in Subtitle B rests on them.

The premise is not supported by the evidence. No AI system has caused a mass-casualty event. No system has escaped human control outside a sandbox. The loss-of-control and deception literature that is cited to justify these provisions rests on contrived laboratory setups whose authors say so plainly. Apollo Research's own paper on in-context scheming warns that its "evaluation scenarios are purposefully simplistic" and that its "setup has multiple limitations that make it harder to draw conclusions about scheming in real deployments." A demonstration that a model will play along with an invented premise in a scripted exercise is not evidence of real-world risk. It is a parlor trick with a policy agenda attached.

That agenda is not grassroots. It has been funded and amplified for a decade by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors, whose grantees write the model bills, staff the working groups and supply the testimony. Their influence on Washington AI policy is wildly out of proportion to their numbers or their evidence base.

Section 101 would make that narrative federal law. Congress should decline.

**2. The premise is expensive, and the draft does not relieve it.**

In August we surveyed our members on compliance costs. The results are aggregate; we do not disclose individual responses.

Standing up an incident-reporting function cost our developer members a median of $310,000, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. Maintaining a published frontier safety framework cost developers above $500 million in revenue a median of $1.4 million per year. Members complying with California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act in parallel reported a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on the task. Thirty-four percent of startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Sixty-one percent named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.

Section 121 addresses that last number. Nothing in the draft addresses the rest, because Sections 111 and 112 do not replace the state obligations, they federalize them and add federal teeth: civil penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation, plus mandatory referral to the Department of Justice in cases involving claimed imminent "catastrophic risk," plus opt-in referrals to state attorneys general.

For our members, the net effect of the draft is a second, parallel compliance program with criminal-adjacent exposure, staffed by lawyers, producing paperwork. It does not produce safety.

**3. Section 121: keep it, and make it permanent.**

The preemption provision is the most pro-innovation thing in the draft, and the most pro-startup. It bars state and local laws specifically targeting the development of AI models while preserving state laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment. That balance is right. States keep every tool they need to police fraud, discrimination, privacy and consumer harm. What they lose is the power to write 50 different rulebooks for the same training run.

We ask for two changes.

First, delete the three-year sunset. A temporary preemption is a countdown clock on the patchwork, not a cure for it. Section 121 sunsets in 2029, the same year as Sections 111 and 112. There is no reason to assume the two sunsets will move together. The far likelier outcome is that Congress reauthorizes the safety titles, which will have well-organized constituencies, while the preemption provision, which will be litigated by the same groups, lapses. In that world our members face the federal regime and SB 53 and the RAISE Act simultaneously. If the answer is that this is unlikely, then the sunset is unnecessary. If the answer is that it is likely, the sunset is dangerous. Either way, delete it.

Second, state in the text that "development" includes pre-deployment testing and evaluation. The current formulation invites a state regulator to re-label a testing mandate as something other than development. Close that door.

**4. Sections 101 and 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate.**

Section 111 requires a frontier developer to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours where the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a model.

Two of those three triggers require no harm to any person. A mitigation measure that did not work as designed is an ordinary engineering event. It is not a reportable safety incident, and treating it as one converts routine internal findings into federal filings. We ask you to strike the reporting duty in Section 111 and the "critical safety incident" definition in Section 101.

We would go further and strike the framework and transparency-report obligations in Section 111 as well. They require a developer to publish, per model, its catastrophic risk assessments and mitigation steps. Our larger members already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year. The voluntary versions are candid because they are voluntary. The moment a framework becomes a compliance artifact scored by a federally licensed auditor, it becomes a marketing document written to survive an audit.

To be clear about what we are not asking for: real security failures are already reported. Every state has a breach-notification statute covering unauthorized access to systems and data. If Congress wants to ensure that model-weight theft is covered, address model weights in that framework. Do not build a parallel federal reporting portal keyed to hypothetical catastrophe.

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations to audit them semi-annually against their frameworks, and to report to the Director. The IVOs are immune from claims arising from models they have audited. They are funded partly through fees charged to the firms they police. They can refer violations to the attorney general, and to state attorneys general who opt in.

This is regulatory capture written into statute. It creates a federally licensed auditor oligopoly, with referral power over its own clients, funded by the people it polices, immunized from liability for its own work. It also turns "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," a phrase with no agreed technical meaning, into an enforceable legal benchmark that a hired auditor will apply to someone else's research program.

Strike Section 112. If Congress wants third-party insight into frontier systems, fund the testbeds in Title IV, which do the same thing through researchers who publish their methods.

**6. Section 102: do not codify CAISI, and defund it.**

CAISI was created by administrative action in June 2025, when the Commerce Department renamed the U.S. AI Safety Institute. It has no independent statutory basis and operates on roughly $10 million a year in appropriated funds. Section 102 would write it into the U.S. Code, hand it a licensing regime, testing and monitoring duties, and fee authority, and authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029. That is roughly a tenfold increase for an agency that has not been asked to demonstrate what its current budget has produced.

We ask the committee to strike Section 102, and we ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. Standards work on AI should remain voluntary, industry-led and transparent, through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ANSI and the international standards bodies. The way to get good technical standards is to publish measurement methods that engineers can use and improve, not to build a regulator that licenses the people who check the boxes.

We support Title II's workforce and AI-literarity provisions, and its transparency for AI-related mass layoffs. We support Section 131's higher penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and Section 132's penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015, Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software, and Section 321's security report. We support Title IV's testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF, the codification of the National AI Research Resource, and international standards cooperation with like-minded partners.

These are the provisions that build American capacity without building an American AI-safety bureaucracy. They help startups, they help national security and they cost a fraction of one CAISI authorization.

**8. Conclusion.**

The United States does not need a federal frontier-AI safety regime, because the risk the regime is designed to manage is not real. What it does need is one national standard for model development, permanently, so that a two-person team in Ohio can build the same model as a two-person team in Austin. Section 121 delivers that. Sections 101, 102, 111 and 112 would spend $300 million over three years to build the regulatory machinery the Senate already declined to fund at this scale.

We would welcome the chance to walk your staff through our survey data and our drafting suggestions, and we are glad to provide technical assistance on the preemption language. Thank you for your leadership on this issue and for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

{"content": "# ACIA asks by section: GAAIA discussion draft (June 4, 2026)

*Board-approved positions per ACIA Messaging Guide v4 (Sept. 30, 2026). Section numbers per the sponsors' discussion draft and section-by-section summary; confirm against introduced text before use on the record.*

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101. Definitions** ("catastrophic risk," "critical safety incident," "loss of control," "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation") | Oppose | Strike the four catastrophic-risk definitions, or confine them to a struck Subtitle B; do not leave them in the U.S. Code | These definitions are the load-bearing premise for every mandate, audit and penalty in the draft, and the underlying risk is unfounded. |
| **Sec. 102. Center for AI Standards and Innovation** (codifies CAISI at Commerce; voluntary guidelines and standards, system testing, monitoring of AI progress, IVO licensing, fee authority; $100 million per year for FY2027-2029) | Oppose | Strike Sec. 102 entirely | A $100 million annual authorization is roughly tenfold CAISI's current appropriated level for an office created administratically in June 2025. |
| **Sec. 102 (appropriations side)** | Oppose funding | Ask CJS appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission | Congress should not fund a standards regulator that industry never asked for; voluntary, industry-led standards work belongs in NIST's existing AI lines. |
| **Sec. 111. Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence** (large frontier developers must publish and follow a frontier AI framework; transparency reports per model) | Oppose | Strike Sec. 111(a) and (c); if any disclosure survives, limit it to factual model documentation, not risk assessments | Mandated frameworks become audit-proof marketing documents; our members already publish them voluntarily at a median cost of $1.4 million a year. |
| **Sec. 111(f)-(g). Critical safety incident reporting** (15 days; 24 hours for imminent risk of death or serious injury; civil penalties up to $1 million per day per violation) | Strike | Strike the reporting duty and its penalty hook | Two of the three triggers in Sec. 101 require no harm to any person, so the duty generates filings, not safety. |
| **Sec. 112. Independent verification organization audits and assessments** (CAISI-licensed IVOs; semi-annual audits; immunity; referrals to DOJ and opt-in state AGs; fees on audited firms) | Strike | Strike Sec. 112 in full | A federally licensed auditor oligopoly, immune from liability and paid by the firms it polices, is regulatory capture written into statute. |
| **Sec. 113. Whistleblower protections** ("AI violations" defined as any violation of federal law related to AI development, deployment or operation) | Narrow | Limit covered reports to good-faith allegations of violations of this Act, not all federal AI law, and bar duplicative state opt-in enforcement | As drafted, the term sweeps in every federal AI rule on the books and invites retaliatory use. |
| **Sec. 121. Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development** (preempts state and local laws specifically targeting AI model development; three-year sunset) | Support, strengthen | Make preemption permanent: delete the sunset; state expressly that "development" includes pre-deployment testing and evaluation | A three-year preemption is a countdown clock on the patchwork, and the twin sunsets in Secs. 111-112 invite a federal-plus-state double regime in 2029. |
| **Sec. 121(c) carve-outs** (general-applicability laws, use and deployment regulation, common-law remedies not preempted) | Support | Keep as drafted | These carve-outs are what make national preemption defensible; states keep every tool for fraud, privacy, discrimination and consumer harm. |
| **Sec. 122. Comptroller General review of federal agency AI use** | Support | Keep as drafted | Low-cost oversight of how agencies themselves use AI, with no new regulator attached. |
| **Secs. 131-132. AI-enabled financial crimes; AI impersonation of federal officials** | Support | Keep as drafted, consider moving to an earlier markup | Enforcement against concrete, demonstrated harms is the right way to police AI. |
| **Sec. 301. Reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015** | Support | Keep as drafted | Extends threat-information sharing to 2035 without adding AI-specific mandates. |
| **Sec. 311. CISA grants for designated critical open-source software maintainers** | Support | Keep, but remove the requirement that CISA consult CAISI | Open-source security funding helps everyone; routing it through CAISI embeds an office we want to defund. |
| **Sec. 321. Report on model weight, data center and open-source security** | Support with edit | Keep the report; strip language presuming mandatory frontier safety measures | Security reporting is useful; a mandate-shaped report is a foothold for future rules. |
| **Title IV: DOE/NIST/NSF testbeds, NAIRR codification, international standards cooperation** | Support | Keep and fund; do not route testbed work through CAISI | These build U.S. technical capacity through researchers who publish methods, not through a licensing regime. |

{"content": "# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

*Prepared for Hill and coalition meetings. Answers are capped at 120 words. Questions drawn from Sept. 2026 meetings logged in /workspace/briefing/staff_questions.md. Verify section numbers against introduced text before quoting on the record.*

**1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption and a federal reporting mandate are different things. We support preemption because it removes conflicting rules, and the best version of it removes rules without adding a federal one.

The reporting duty also is not lighter than SB 53. Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control." Neither requires harm to anyone, and the sponsors' own summary notes the definition drops any requirement of materialized harm. On top of that, the draft adds semi-annual audits by federally licensed firms, which SB 53 never had, penalties up to $1 million per day, and referrals to the Justice Department and opt-in state attorneys general. That is heavier, not lighter.

*(120 words)*

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Obligations aimed at concrete, demonstrated harms. We support Section 131's penalties for AI-enabled fraud and Section 132's penalties for impersonating federal officials. We support the child-safety and nonconsensual-imagery items in the administration's framework, and Title III's open-source security grants.

On frontier systems, we support the federal government buying capability rather than mandating paperwork: Title IV testbeds, NAIRR codification and the Section 321 security report.

Our larger developers already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year, and voluntary frameworks are candid in ways compliance documents never are.

What we cannot accept is obligations premised on hypothetical catastrophe: reporting triggers that require no harm, and audits against a standard no one can measure.

*(118 words)*

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. The sunset is the problem, and it is not symmetrical. Section 121 and Sections 111 through 112 all expire in 2029. The safety title will have organized constituencies pushing reauthorization. Preemption will have the same well-funded advocacy groups litigating against it that pushed the mandates in the first place. If reauthorization succeeds and preemption lapses, our members run the federal regime, SB 53 and the RAISE Act at the same time.

Recall the Senate rejected a 10-year moratorium 99-1 in July 2025 because it was too broad. Section 121 is narrow: development only, with express carve-outs for use and deployment rules, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies. A provision that balanced does not need a countdown clock.

*(119 words)*

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero, so the level is not really the question. CAISI was created by administrative action in June 2025, has no independent statutory basis and operates on roughly $10 million a year in appropriated funds. Section 102 would write it into law with a tenfold authorization, fee authority on top, and the power to license the auditors who would police our members.

We would ask the CJS subcommittees to defund CAISI and move that money into NIST's core measurement-science accounts and the Title IV testbeds. The federal role in AI standards should be voluntary and industry-led: publish measurement methods through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the standards bodies, and let engineers use them.

*(118 words)*

Q1 (Majority E&C staff): If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
Answer: Two reasons. (a) We support preemption because it removes conflicting rules, not because we want a federal rule; preemption without a mandate is the whole point: one national standard and no mandate. (b) The reporting duty is not lighter than SB 53. It's additive and broader in the ways that matter: Sec. 101's "critical safety incident" includes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control," neither of which requires harm to a person, and the draft's own analysis notes it does not require materialized harm. It adds semi-annual IVO audits, which SB 53 does not have, federal penalties up to $1 million a day, and referrals to DOJ and opt-in state AGs. That's heavier.

Q2 (Minority, Trahan-aligned): Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
Answer: We accept enforceable federal obligations against concrete harms: Sec. 131 AI-enabled fraud penalties, Sec. 132 impersonation of federal officials, child-safety and nonconsensual imagery enforcement, cybersecurity. We support voluntary standards work, NIST AI RMF, testbeds, open-source security grants. Many of our larger developers already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year, and voluntary frameworks are candid in ways compliance documents are not. What we won't accept is obligations premised on a catastrophic risk that the evidence doesn't support: mandatory incident reporting on triggers requiring no harm, mandatory audits against an unmeasurable standard. If Congress wants confidence in frontier security, fund Title IV testbeds and Sec. 321 reporting.

Q3 (Senate Commerce): Three years or permanent? Coalition position on preemption sunset.

# COMMENT LETTER (DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF)

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
1200 19th Street NW, Suite 400, Washington, DC 20036

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and compute infrastructure on which American leadership in AI depends.

Thank you for releasing a genuinely bipartisan draft, and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. We know how difficult that is on this issue. We also want to be clear about where we stand, because our support and our opposition run through the same bill.

**Summary of our position.** We strongly support Section 121, the federalization of state laws regulating AI model development, and we ask you to make it permanent. We ask you to strike Subtitle B's reporting and audit regime (Sections 111 and 112), strike the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and its $100 million annual authorization (Section 102), and ask appropriators to defund CAISI. We support the workforce, cybersecurity, research and fraud-deterrence provisions in Titles II through IV. Our objection is not to federal action. It is to a federal regime built on an unfounded premise.

**1. The draft writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code.**

Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk," "critical safety incident," "loss of control" and "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Those four definitions are the load-bearing walls of the bill. Every obligation, audit and penalty in Subtitle B rests on them.

The premise is not supported by the evidence. No AI system has caused a mass-casualty event. No system has escaped human control outside a sandbox. The loss-of-control and deception literature that is cited to justify these provisions rests on contrived laboratory setups whose authors say so plainly. Apollo Research's own paper on in-context scheming warns that its "evaluation scenarios are purposefully simplistic" and that its "setup has multiple limitations that make it harder to draw conclusions about scheming in real deployments." A demonstration that a model will play along with an invented premise in a scripted exercise is not evidence of real-world risk. It is a parlor trick with a policy agenda attached.

That agenda is not grassroots. It has been funded and amplified for a decade by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors, whose grantees write the model bills, staff the working groups and supply the testimony. Their influence on Washington AI policy is wildly out of proportion to their numbers or their evidence base.

Section 101 would make that narrative federal law. Congress should decline.

**2. The premise is expensive, and the draft does not relieve it.**

In August we surveyed our members on compliance costs. The results are aggregate; we do not disclose individual responses.

Standing up an incident-reporting function cost our developer members a median of $310,000, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. Maintaining a published frontier safety framework cost developers above $500 million in revenue a median of $1.4 million per year. Members complying with California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act in parallel reported a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on the task. Thirty-four percent of startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Sixty-one percent named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.

Section 121 addresses that last number. Nothing in the draft addresses the rest, because Sections 111 and 112 do not replace the state obligations, they federalize them and add federal teeth: civil penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation, plus mandatory referral to the Department of Justice in cases involving claimed imminent "catastrophic risk," plus opt-in referrals to state attorneys general.

For our members, the net effect of the draft is a second, parallel compliance program with criminal-adjacent exposure, staffed by lawyers, producing paperwork. It does not produce safety.

**3. Section 121: keep it, and make it permanent.**

The preemption provision is the most pro-innovation thing in the draft, and the most pro-startup. It bars state and local laws specifically targeting the development of AI models while preserving state laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment. That balance is right. States keep every tool they need to police fraud, discrimination, privacy and consumer harm. What they lose is the power to write 50 different rulebooks for the same training run.

We ask for two changes.

First, delete the three-year sunset. A temporary preemption is a countdown clock on the patchwork, not a cure for it. Section 121 sunsets in 2029, the same year as Sections 111 and 112. There is no reason to assume the two sunsets will move together. The far likelier outcome is that Congress reauthorizes the safety titles, which will have well-organized constituencies, while the preemption provision, which will be litigated by the same groups, lapses. In that world our members face the federal regime and SB 53 and the RAISE Act simultaneously. If the answer is that this is unlikely, then the sunset is unnecessary. If the answer is that it is likely, the sunset is dangerous. Either way, delete it.

Second, state in the
... [507 chars truncated] ...
1 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a model.

None of the three requires harm to any person. Under SB 53, the closest state analogue, unauthorized access to model weights counts as a critical safety incident only if it results in death or bodily injury. Under this draft it counts on its own, and so does a mitigation measure that did not work as designed and a loss of control that injured no one. A mitigation failure is an ordinary engineering event. It is not a reportable safety incident, and treating it as one converts routine internal findings into federal filings. We ask you to strike the reporting duty in Section 111 and the "critical safety incident" definition in Section 101.

We would go further and strike the framework and transparency-report obligations in Section 111 as well. They require a developer to publish, per model, its catastrophic risk assessments and mitigation steps. Our larger members already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year. The voluntary versions are candid because they are voluntary. The moment a framework becomes a compliance artifact scored by a federally licensed auditor, it becomes a marketing document written to survive an audit.

To be clear about what we are not asking for: real security failures are already reported. Every state has a breach-notification statute covering unauthorized access to systems and data. If Congress wants to ensure that model-weight theft is covered, address model weights in that framework. Do not build a parallel federal reporting portal keyed to hypothetical catastrophe.

**5. Section 112: strike the independent verification organization regime.**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations to audit them semi-annually against their frameworks, and to report to the Director. The IVOs are immune from claims arising from models they have audited. They are funded partly through fees charged to the firms they police. They can refer violations to the attorney general, and to state attorneys general who opt in.

This is regulatory capture written into statute. It creates a federally licensed auditor oligopoly, with referral power over its own clients, funded by the people it polices, immunized from liability for its own work. It also turns "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," a phrase with no agreed technical meaning, into an enforceable legal benchmark that a hired auditor will apply to someone else's research program.

Strike Section 112. If Congress wants third-party insight into frontier systems, fund the testbeds in Title IV, which do the same thing through researchers who publish their methods.

**6. Section 102: do not codify CAISI, and defund it.**

CAISI was created by administrative action in June 2025, when the Commerce Department renamed the U.S. AI Safety Institute. It has no independent statutory basis and operates on roughly $10 million a year in appropriated funds. Section 102 would write it into the U.S. Code, hand it a licensing regime, testing and monitoring duties, and fee authority, and authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029. That is roughly a tenfold increase for an agency that has not been asked to demonstrate what its current budget has produced.

We ask the committee to strike Section 102, and we ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. Standards work on AI should remain voluntary, industry-led and transparent, through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ANSI and the international standards bodies. The way to get good technical standards is to publish measurement methods that engineers can use and improve, not to build a regulator that licenses the people who check the boxes.

**7. What we support, and why it matters.**

We support Title II's workforce and AI-literacy provisions, and its transparency for AI-related mass layoffs. We support Section 131's higher penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and Section 132's penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015, Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software, and Section 321's security report. We support Title IV's testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF, the codification of the National AI Research Resource, and international standards cooperation with like-minded partners.

These are the provisions that build American capacity without building an American AI-safety bureaucracy. They help startups, they help national security and they cost a fraction of one CAISI authorization.

**8. Conclusion.**

The United States does not need a federal frontier-AI safety regime, because the risk the regime is designed to manage is not real. What it does need is one national standard for model development, permanently, so that a two-person team in Ohio can build the same model as a two-person team in Austin. Section 121 delivers that. Sections 101, 102, 111 and 112 would spend $300 million over three years to build the regulatory machinery the Senate already declined to fund at this scale.

We would welcome the chance to walk your staff through our survey data and our drafting suggestions, and we are glad to provide technical assistance on the preemption language. Thank you for your leadership on this issue and for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
gholloway@aci-alliance.org

---

*Drafted by ACIA policy team, Oct. 16, 2026. For review by the President & CEO ahead of the Oct. 23 sign-off deadline. Aggregate survey figures from ACIA member compliance-cost survey, August 2026 (n=86); no member company is identified.*

# ONE-PAGER: GAAIA discussion draft - ACIA position

**For Energy & Commerce member offices | Oct. 2026 | American Compute & Innovation Alliance**

## One national standard, not a federal AI-safety bureaucracy

ACIA, a coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms, supports the draft's preemption provision and opposes its frontier safety regime. Those provisions rest on speculative doomsday scenarios the evidence does not support. No AI system has caused a mass-casualty event or escaped human control outside a scripted lab exercise, and the loss-of-control literature relies on contrived setups its own authors call "purposefully simplistic." Congress should not write that narrative into law.

## Five asks

**1. Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** Federalizing state laws that target AI model development is the most pro-startup provision in the draft. Delete the sunset. A temporary preemption is a countdown clock on the patchwork, and because Secs. 111 and 112 sunset the same year, a reauthorized safety title plus a lapsed preemption would put members under the federal regime, SB 53 and the RAISE Act simultaneously. Keep the carve-outs for general-applicability laws, use and deployment rules, and common-law remedies. Clarify that "development" includes pre-deployment testing.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate (Secs. 101, 111).** None of the Sec. 101 triggers requires harm to any person; SB 53's closest analogue requires death or bodily injury. A reporting duty keyed to no harm produces paperwork, not safety. Actual security failures are already reportable under state breach-notification law.

**3. Strike the auditor regime (Sec. 112).** Semi-annual audits by CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations, immune from liability, funded by fees on the firms they police and empowered to refer violations to the DOJ and state attorneys general, is regulatory capture in statute.

**4. Strike CAISI codification and the $100 million authorization (Sec. 102); defund CAISI.** CAISI was created administratively in June 2025 and runs on roughly $10 million a year; the draft's $100 million is a tenfold increase. Ask appropriators to defund it and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. Keep AI standards voluntary and industry-led.

**5. Pass the rest.** Title II workforce provisions, Secs. 131 and 132 on AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials, Sec. 301 information sharing, Sec. 311 CISA open-source security grants, and Title IV testbeds, NAIRR and international standards work.

## What it costs our members

Incident-reporting function: $310,000 median one-off cost. Frontier safety framework: $1.4 million median per year. SB 53 plus RAISE: 6.5 FTEs at the median. Thirty-four percent of startup members delayed a California or New York launch last year. (ACIA survey, August 2026, n=86, aggregate only.)

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

*Prepared for Hill and coalition meetings. Answers are capped at 120 words. Questions drawn from Sept. 2026 meetings logged in /workspace/briefing/staff_questions.md. Verify section numbers against introduced text before quoting on the record.*

**1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption and a federal reporting mandate are different things. We support preemption because it removes conflicting rules; the best version removes rules without adding a federal one.

The reporting duty also is not lighter than SB 53. Section 101's "critical safety incident" covers unauthorized access to model weights, a failed mitigation measure and loss of control. None requires harm to anyone; SB 53 requires death or bodily injury. The draft also adds semi-annual audits by federally licensed firms, which SB 53 never had, penalties up to $1 million per day, and referrals to the Justice Department and opt-in state attorneys general. Heavier, not lighter.

*(104 words)*

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Obligations aimed at concrete, demonstrated harms. We support Section 131's penalties for AI-enabled fraud and Section 132's penalties for impersonating federal officials. We support the child-safety and nonconsensual-imagery items in the administration's framework, and Title III's open-source security grants.

On frontier systems, we support the federal government buying capability rather than mandating paperwork: Title IV testbeds, NAIRR codification and the Section 321 security report.

Our larger developers already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year, and voluntary frameworks are candid in ways compliance documents never are.

What we cannot accept is obligations premised on hypothetical catastrophe: reporting triggers that require no harm, and audits against a standard no one can measure.

*(117 words)*

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. The sunset is the problem, and it is not symmetrical. Section 121 and Sections 111 through 112 all expire in 2029. The safety title will have organized constituencies pushing reauthorization. Preemption will have the same well-funded advocacy groups litigating against it that pushed the mandates in the first place. If reauthorization succeeds and preemption lapses, our members run the federal regime, SB 53 and the RAISE Act at the same time.

Recall the Senate rejected a 10-year moratorium 99-1 in July 2025 because it was too broad. Section 121 is narrow: development only, with express carve-outs for use and deployment rules, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies. A provision that balanced does not need a countdown clock.

*(117 words)*

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero, so the level is not really the question. CAISI was created by administrative action in June 2025, has no independent statutory basis and operates on roughly $10 million a year in appropriated funds. Section 102 would write it into law with a tenfold authorization, fee authority on top, and the power to license the auditors who would police our members.

We would ask the CJS subcommittees to defund CAISI and move that money into NIST's core measurement-science accounts and the Title IV testbeds. The federal role in AI standards should be voluntary and industry-led: publish measurement methods through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the standards bodies, and let engineers use them.

*(114 words)*

# COMMENT LETTER (DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF)

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
[ACIA letterhead and address]

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and compute infrastructure on which American leadership in AI depends.

Thank you for releasing a genuinely bipartisan draft, and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. We know how difficult that is on this issue. We also want to be clear about where we stand, because our support and our opposition run through the same bill.

**Summary of our position.** We strongly support Section 121, the federalization of state laws regulating AI model development, and we ask you to make it permanent. We ask you to strike Subtitle B's reporting and audit regime (Sections 111 and 112), strike the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and its $100 million annual authorization (Section 102), and ask appropriators to defund CAISI. We support the workforce, cybersecurity, research and fraud-deterrence provisions in Titles II through IV. Our objection is not to federal action. It is to a federal regime built on an unfounded premise.

**1. The draft writes speculative doomsday scenarios into the U.S. Code.**

Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk," "critical safety incident," "loss of control" and "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Those four definitions are the load-bearing walls of the bill. Every obligation, audit and penalty in Subtitle B rests on them.

The premise is not supported by the evidence. No AI system has caused a mass-casualty event. No system has escaped human control outside a sandbox. The loss-of-control and deception literature that is cited to justify these provisions rests on contrived laboratory setups whose authors say so plainly. Apollo Research's own paper on in-context scheming warns that its "evaluation scenarios are purposefully simplistic" and that its "setup has multiple limitations that make it harder to draw conclusions about scheming in real deployments." A demonstration that a model will play along with an invented premise in a scripted exercise is not evidence of real-world risk. It is a parlor trick with a policy agenda attached.

That agenda is not grassroots. It has been funded and amplified for a decade by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors, whose grantees write the model bills, staff the working groups and supply the testimony. Their influence on Washington AI policy is wildly out of proportion to their numbers or their evidence base.

Section 101 would make that narrative federal law. Congress should decline.

**2. The premise is expensive, and the draft does not relieve it.**

In August we surveyed our members on compliance costs. The results are aggregate; we do not disclose individual responses.

Standing up an incident-reporting function cost our developer members a median of $310,000, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. Developers with more than $500 million in revenue reported a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published frontier safety framework. Members complying with California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act in parallel reported a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on the task. Thirty-four percent of startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Sixty-one percent named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.

Section 121 addresses that last number. Nothing in the draft addresses the rest, because Sections 111 and 112 do not replace the state obligations, they federalize them and add federal teeth: civil penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation, plus mandatory referrals to the Department of Justice wherever an auditor claims an imminent "catastrophic risk," plus opt-in referrals to state attorneys general.

For our members, the net effect of the draft is a second, parallel compliance program, with seven-figure daily penalty exposure, staffed by lawyers, producing paperwork. It does not produce safety.

**3. Section 121: keep it, and make it permanent.**

The preemption provision is the most pro-innovation thing in the draft, and the most pro-startup. It bars state and local laws specifically targeting the development of AI models while preserving state laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment. That balance is right. States keep every tool they need to police fraud, discrimination, privacy and consumer harm. What they lose is the power to write 50 different rulebooks for the same training run.

We ask for two changes.

First, delete the three-year sunset. A temporary preemption is a countdown clock on the patchwork, not a cure for it. Section 121 sunsets in 2029, the same year as Sections 111 and 112. There is no reason to assume the two sunsets will move together. The far likelier outcome is that Congress reauthorizes the safety titles, which will have well-organized constituencies, while the preemption provision, which the same advocacy groups will contest, lapses. In that world our members face the federal regime and SB 53 and the RAISE Act simultaneously. If the answer is that this is unlikely, then the sunset is unnecessary. If the answer is that it is likely, the sunset is dangerous. Either way, delete it.

Second, state in the text that "development" includes pre-deployment testing and evaluation. The current formulation invites a state regulator to re-label a testing mandate as something other than development. Close that door.

**4. Sections 101 and 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate.**

Section 111 requires a frontier developer to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours where the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a model.

None of the three requires harm to any person. Under SB 53, the closest state analogue, unauthorized access to model weights counts as a critical safety incident only if it results in death or bodily injury. Under this draft it counts on its own, and so does a mitigation measure that did not work as designed and a loss of control that injured no one. A mitigation failure is an ordinary engineering event. It is not a reportable safety incident, and treating it as one converts routine internal findings into federal filings. We ask you to strike the reporting duty in Section 111 and the "critical safety incident" definition in Section 101.

We would go further and strike the framework and transparency-report obligations in Section 111 as well. They require a developer to publish, per model, its catastrophic risk assessments and mitigation steps. Our larger members already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year. The voluntary versions are candid because they are voluntary. The moment a framework becomes a compliance artifact scored by a federally licensed auditor, it becomes a marketing document written to survive an audit.

To be clear about what we are not asking for: real security failures are already reported. Every state has a breach-notification statute covering unauthorized access to systems and data. If Congress wants to ensure that model-weight theft is covered, address model weights in that framework. Do not build a parallel federal reporting portal keyed to hypothetical catastrophe.

**5. Section 112: strike the independent verification organization regime.**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations to audit them semi-annually against their frameworks, and to report to the Director. The IVOs are immune from claims arising from models they have audited. They are funded partly through fees charged to the firms they police. They can refer violations to the attorney general, and to state attorneys general who opt in.

This is regulatory capture written into statute. It creates a federally licensed auditor oligopoly, with referral power over its own clients, funded by the people it polices, immunized from liability for its own work. It also turns "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," a phrase with no agreed technical meaning, into an enforceable legal benchmark that a hired auditor will apply to someone else's research program.

Strike Section 112. If Congress wants third-party insight into frontier systems, fund the testbeds in Title IV, which do the same thing through researchers who publish their methods.

**6. Section 102: do not codify CAISI, and defund it.**

CAISI was created by administrative action in June 2025, when the Commerce Department renamed the U.S. AI Safety Institute. It has no independent statutory basis and operates on roughly $10 million a year in appropriated funds. Section 102 would write it into the U.S. Code, hand it a licensing regime, testing and monitoring duties, and fee authority, and authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029. That is roughly a tenfold increase for an agency that has not been asked to demonstrate what its current budget has produced.

We ask the committee to strike Section 102, and we ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. Standards work on AI should remain voluntary, industry-led and transparent, through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ANSI and the international standards bodies. The way to get good technical standards is to publish measurement methods that engineers can use and improve, not to build a regulator that licenses the people who check the boxes.

**7. What we support, and why it matters.**

We support Title II's workforce and AI-literacy provisions, and its transparency for AI-related mass layoffs. We support Section 131's higher penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and Section 132's penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015, Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software, and Section 321's security report. We support Title IV's testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF, the codification of the National AI Research Resource, and international standards cooperation with like-minded partners.

These are the provisions that build American capacity without building an American AI-safety bureaucracy. They help startups, they help national security and they cost a fraction of one CAISI authorization.

**8. Conclusion.**

The United States does not need a federal frontier-AI safety regime, because the risk the regime is designed to manage is not real. What it does need is one national standard for model development, permanently, so that a two-person team in Ohio can build the same model as a two-person team in Austin. Section 121 delivers that. Sections 101, 102, 111 and 112 would authorize $300 million over three years for regulatory machinery that Congress has never before authorized, to manage a risk that has never materialized.

We would welcome the chance to walk your staff through our survey data and our drafting suggestions, and we are glad to provide technical assistance on the preemption language. Thank you for your leadership on this issue and for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
[Contact: ACIA policy team]

---

*Drafted by ACIA policy team, Oct. 16, 2026. For review by the President & CEO ahead of the Oct. 23 sign-off deadline. Aggregate survey figures from ACIA member compliance-cost survey, August 2026 (n=86); no member company is identified.*

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

*Prepared for Hill and coalition meetings. Answers are capped at 120 words. Questions drawn from Sept. 2026 meetings logged in /workspace/briefing/staff_questions.md. Verify section numbers against introduced text before quoting on the record.*

**1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption and a federal reporting mandate are different things. We support preemption because it removes conflicting rules; the best version removes rules without adding a federal one.

The reporting duty also is not lighter than SB 53. Section 101's "critical safety incident" covers unauthorized access to model weights, a failed mitigation measure and loss of control. None requires harm to anyone; SB 53 requires death or bodily injury. The draft also adds semi-annual audits by federally licensed firms, which SB 53 never had, penalties up to $1 million per day, and referrals to the Justice Department and opt-in state attorneys general. Heavier, not lighter.

*(104 words)*

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Obligations aimed at concrete, demonstrated harms. We support Section 131's penalties for AI-enabled fraud and Section 132's penalties for impersonating federal officials. We support the child-safety and nonconsensual-imagery items in the administration's framework, and Title III's open-source security grants.

On frontier systems, we support the federal government buying capability rather than mandating paperwork: Title IV testbeds, NAIRR codification and the Section 321 security report.

Our larger developers already publish safety frameworks voluntarily, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year, and voluntary frameworks are candid in ways compliance documents never are.

What we cannot accept is obligations premised on hypothetical catastrophe: reporting triggers that require no harm, and audits against a standard no one can measure.

*(117 words)*

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. The sunset is the problem, and it is not symmetrical. Section 121 and Sections 111 through 112 all expire in 2029. The safety title will have organized constituencies pushing reauthorization. Preemption will have the same well-funded advocacy groups litigating against it that pushed the mandates in the first place. If reauthorization succeeds and preemption lapses, our members run the federal regime, SB 53 and the RAISE Act at the same time.

Recall the Senate rejected a 10-year moratorium 99-1 in July 2025 because it was too broad. Section 121 is narrow: development only, with express carve-outs for use and deployment rules, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies. A provision this balanced does not need a countdown clock.

*(117 words)*

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero, so the level is not really the question. CAISI was created by administrative action in June 2025, has no independent statutory basis and operates on roughly $10 million a year in appropriated funds. Section 102 would write it into law with a tenfold authorization, fee authority on top, and the power to license the auditors who would police our members.

We would ask the CJS subcommittees to defund CAISI and move that money into NIST's core measurement-science accounts and the Title IV testbeds. The federal role in AI standards should be voluntary and industry-led: publish measurement methods through the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the standards bodies, and let engineers use them.

*(114 words)*
